findings.problem: start 1583 is a birth year. The row item it replaces sits after Jacobus Arminius (1603) in the-remonstrants-and-dort people row. The validator orders a person item by its start (tools/validate-census.mjs line 159, 'yearOf'), so replacing the item in place fails 'the people list is not in date order'. Reordering the row would put Grotius before Arminius, which misleads. Every release 29 person entry uses sourced working years, not birth years (origen c. 203-253, john-calvin 1536-1564).

findings.fix: Use working years from the 1617 Defence to his death: dates '1617-1645', start 1617, end 1645. The fact-table row cites Foster line 364 for 1617 and line 2 for 1645. Teaser: 'Leiden and the Netherlands, 1617 to 1645.' The row order then stays Arminius 1603, Grotius 1617.

findings.problem: 'his one treatise on theology from the quarrel years' and 'the leading jurist on the Remonstrant side in the States of Holland' rest only on the Library thread's own header Content note (line 8). That is catalogue metadata the project wrote, not a source. Nothing in Foster's text supports 'one'. 'In 1617, at Leiden, he wrote' also turns the place of the first edition into the place of writing.
findings.evidence: Foster file line 8 (header Content note) is the only citation. Foster's own text gives only 'first edition, Leyden, 1617' (line 364). It gives no count of Grotius's theological works and no rank among the jurists.
findings.fix: longDescription paragraph 1: 'Grotius was a jurist of Holland on the Remonstrant side. In 1617 he published at Leiden a treatise on theology. It answers Faustus Socinus, who denied that Christ's death satisfied divine justice.' why: 'In 1617 he published at Leiden a defence of the doctrine that ...'. Cite Foster 364 and 756-757 ('his fellow-Arminians'). Drop 'one' and 'leading'.

findings.problem: The legacy says Baxter 'named him on both sides', and frames the lying passage with 'Yet he also'. In that passage Baxter rejects what Grotius wrote in De Jure Belli. That is a second criticism, not praise, so 'both sides' misleads. The floorNote sets 'Baxter said he had turned Papist' against 'His treatise defends the church's doctrine against Socinus' as if these were the two sides. They are not opposites. The real other side is in the same Baxter passage: Thomas Pierce defended Grotius as 'a judicious peaceable Protestant'.
findings.evidence: cic/texts/baxter_reliquiae-baxterianae_sylvester1696.txt:23646-23651 'having written somewhat in Defence of Grotius, as a judicious peaceable Protestant ... I did thereupon write a little Collection ... to prove him to have turned Papist'; line 51478 'nor do I believe Lying lawful after all that Grotius de Jure Belli ... have said for it'.
findings.fix: legacy: '... Baxter wrote against him twice. He warned the Episcopal party against "Grotianism". When Thomas Pierce defended Grotius as a peaceable Protestant, Baxter collected his late writings to prove he had turned Papist. He also rejected what Grotius had written in favour of lying.' The contested claim then names both sides (Pierce: Protestant; Baxter: Papist). For floorNote see B4.

findings.problem: floorNote is the doctrinal-floor note. It says whether the person stands within the faith the Nicene Creed states. Every release 29 person entry uses it that way ('Not in question.', or why a creed question is or is not raised: nestorius, peter-the-iberian). Four drafts put other caveats there instead. Patrick's is about his dates. Justinian's is about hostile sources. Bede's is about his bias. Grotius's is about the Papist charge. On the page this reads as a floor judgment, which misleads.
findings.evidence: Census person entries' floorNote values (augustine-of-hippo 'Not in question. He wrote On the Trinity ...', john-calvin 'Not in question.'); cft-website/index.html floorNote values for movements ('Nothing in this tradition's confession diverges from the doctrine the Nicene Creed states.').
findings.fix: Set floorNote to 'Not in question.' for all four. Move the caveats where they belong. Patrick's dates caveat goes into sourcing: '... His dates are not his own; they are the reckoning White's 1920 edition reports, and the old lives add details his letters never give.' Justinian's caveat about hostile sources goes into sourcing or the longDescription's last paragraph. Bede's caveat goes into sourcing; see also M7. Grotius's dispute is already in legacy (B3).

findings.problem: 'Thin. The Library holds three of his letters' is wrong. Mirbt's source book alone gives him a run of numbered documents. They include letters of 1198 and 1199 on oaths and on Metz, the 1198 letter, the 1204 ruling on disputes between kingdoms, the canons of the Fourth Lateran Council (yearly confession among them) and his 1215 bull against Magna Carta. Theiner prints many more of his letters by pontifical year, 1204 to 1211. The facts about the Fourth Lateran Council are therefore in a vendored text, not only in the census.

findings.problem: The entry presents the Dictatus Papae as part of Gregory's own record ('In 1075 the Dictatus Papae set down ...'; voice line 'pope of the Dictatus Papae'). The flag says the prose treats it as his. Mirbt's own heading for the text cites Sackur's view that its author was Cardinal Deusdedit. Under answer C, a work of disputed authorship does not count as the person's own words. The contested authorship has to be named, with both sides.
findings.evidence: cic/texts/mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt:11186-11189 '255. Die Rechte des Papstes nach den Grundsätzen d. gregorian. Partei. Dictatus papae Gregorii VII., Registri II 55 a ... ESackur ...: Verfasser Kardinal Deusdedit (gest. c. 1099)'.
findings.fix: longDescription paragraph 2: 'A list of papal claims, the Dictatus Papae, is entered in his Register for 1075. One says the pope may depose emperors. Another says no one may judge him. Mirbt notes Sackur's view that Cardinal Deusdedit wrote it.' why: 'A list of papal claims in his Register for 1075 ...'. voices: 'Gregory VII — pope whose 1076 sentence on Henry IV and report on Canossa the Library holds'. findings.problem: The 1198 letter is rendered without its key clauses. These are 'the greater to rule the day, the lesser the night', 'the greater over souls, as days, the lesser over bodies, as nights', and the moon 'truly less than [the sun] in size and quality, in place and in effect'. The hierarchy the letter argues is the point of the image, and the rendering drops it.
findings.fix: 'God, the maker of all things, set two great lights in the sky, he says. The greater rules the day and the lesser the night. In the same way he set two great offices in the church. The greater rules souls, as if they were days. The lesser rules bodies, as if they were nights. These are the papal authority and the royal power.' Paragraph 2: 'The moon takes its light from the sun, he goes on, and is truly less than it in size and quality, in place and in effect. In the same way, royal power takes the splendour of its rank from the papal authority.'

The home record and the census map that island to both Ireland and the United Kingdom, and Patrick's letters name only 'Ireland'.

findings.problem: 'what he says of its rivals rests on him alone' overclaims. The Library holds the Britons' own Gildas and Nennius, which Bede's own links cite. Jane's 1903 notice says the History is 'practically the only authority for the history of England from the Saxon invasion to the year 732'. It does not say 'the English church'.
findings.fix: Where the caveat moves (B4): 'His History is practically the only record of England to 732, so much of what it says rests on him alone. He was not neutral about the Britons.'
